newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-BOWE IN THE FIGHT OF HIS LIFE.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-BOWE IN THE FIGHT OF HIS LIFE.

text.p: Riddick Bowe is in the fight of his career Saturday.

"It's a crossroads fight for Riddick," said Lou DiBella, vice-president of HBO sports which is broadcasting the pay-per-view bout, of Bowe's rematch against Andrew Golota at the Atlantic City Convention Centre.

"It's the fight that could determine if he is reestablished as the best heavyweight in the world or if he is an afterthought and contemplating retirement," DiBella said of the former two-time champion at a news conference Wednesday.
"If he walks in and Golota takes him out, that could be the end for Riddick. I think this fight is everything for Riddick Bowe," DiBella said.

Bowe (39-1) is in a precarious situation because of what happened six months ago in his first fight against Golota (28-1) at Madison Square Garden. Golota was hammering the 10-1 favourite Bowe all around the ring and was comfortably leading on all the scorecards before being disqualified in the seventh round for repeated low blows.

"Many, many people wrote him off because of that performance," said Bowe's promoter Rock Newman. "There were people who were wondering if he was just going to saunter off, wander into the sunset, never to be heard from again.
"Now here we have the opportunity for Riddick to rise to the occasion in the defining moment in his life," said Newman.
Golota's disqualification touched off a near riot inside and outside the ring.
That night also may have touched off some soul searching for the 29-year-old, Brooklyn-born Bowe.
"Golota has embarrassed, humilated me," Bowe said of the Polish-born heavyweight who has lived in Chicago since 1991.
"I went back and worked on everything, ran a little longer and harder, anything you could think of we came back and worked on," Bowe said of his extended three-month training camp.

"From day 1 he got in here (training camp), his commitment and dedication has been obvious," Newman said. "That is largely attributed to his attitude. He is on mission. He learned a lesson from it. He is back on top of his game."

For the first fight Bowe lumbered in at a career high 252 pounds. At Thursday's weigh-in, Bowe weighed 235, the lightest he has been since the first of his three fights against Evander Holyfield four years ago. Golota was at his usual 239 pounds.

"The first fight you could count the jabs I threw at Golota," said Bowe, who according to CompuBox statistics landed just 47 percent of his jabs and only 40 percent of all his punches in the first fight.
"You could count the number of times I was aggressive," Bowe said. "I was a stationary target. This time you won't see that. I'll have better movement, better hand speed."
The Golota camp rejects Bowe's claims that being fitter will make any difference.
"It is the same man," Golota said. "He doesn't change his style. He may be stronger, but he is the same man."
Said Golota's lead trainer Roger Bloodworth: "I don't think it makes any difference because he is still fat at 235. He looks soft around the middle."
Bowe has also worked on his attitude, something that was in equally bad shape for the July 11 bout.
"The first time I didn't know much about him, I took Golota for granted," Bowe said. "He came ready. I was bewildered. He came to fight. This time both will come to fight."
Bowe's performance and related attitude six months ago was so shockingly bad, it prompted trainer Eddie Futch to walk away, severing a relationship that had started when he had turned pro in 1989.
"Life goes on," said Bowe, who is being trained by Futch's assistant Thel Torrence. "I fought a couple of times without Eddie and I did well."
While others say he has to win the fight, Bowe doesn't agree.
"I'm going to go out there and fight my fight and let the chips fall where they may," Bowe said.
"People have said things about me from the beginning and because they say that it doesn't mean it's true.
"I'm going to keep on keeping on."
